title: Prologue — Tham Jai
paragraphs: The book begins at its ending. In a Chiang Mai hospital, doctors tell Mae San, Paw Nui, and Gaew that Sen's liver is beyond saving. A nurse gives the family its instruction — tham jai, "make your heart" — and they bring him home to Mae Jaeng by ambulance, over the mountains, to die among friends.

At his bedside the town's two kinds of medicine work side by side: Moh Bom, the head doctor, administers what medicine remains, while Nan Jon, the spirit doctor, performs the rite that detaches the spirits of alcohol from Sen's body. Family and friends resolve, in a phrase Julia will hear for years afterward, to let go.

It is Sen's thirty-fifth birthday — and his little brother Noi's twelfth, for they share the day. The family eats grilled pork and cake at the town's one restaurant, speaks of karma, and goes to the monastery to make merit. Only Dee, a niece flown in from England, is audibly distraught, asking the question a Western reader is asking too: why did no one make him stop?

Julia, the anthropologist narrating, puts a version of that question to Moh Bom. His answer gives the book its master concept: anicca — impermanence. "Everything is impermanent," he tells her. "You have to make your heart."

The Prologue then rewinds a decade to explain how she came to be standing in that room: a psychology degree, travels in Asia, a Chiang Mai coffee-shop stranger's paradox that country people "don't really understand Buddhism" and yet "really get it," and a rainy-season motorbike ride west over the mountains to a valley town of five hundred households where she would return, again and again, for ten years.

Everything that follows — the cool hearts, the festivals of letting go, the karma debates, and Sen's long decline and stranger recovery — happens in the shadow of this opening scene. The reader, like the town, knows the ending; the question is what it means.
